questions.title: Keep a production chaos experiment from becoming an incident
questions.prompt: You run a chaos experiment in production. One model provider returns rate-limit errors for part of the fleet, so that you can watch the fallback. Alerts start to fire while it runs. Design the safety plane that keeps this from turning into an incident, and explain how on-call tells an experiment failure from a natural one.
questions.short: Three guards sit in the safety plane: a burn-rate alert that pauses the experiment when the daily error-budget burn passes twice the expected rate, suppression windows that silence the non-experiment alerts inside the blast radius, and a tag on the trace id of every error that the experiment causes. On-call reads the tag. An untagged error inside the window is natural and gets the normal response.
questions.full:
### The planes

The lesson splits the system into a control plane that schedules the experiment, a target plane of services, pods and data stores, a safety plane with the kill switch, suppression windows, blast-radius limits and error-budget gates, and an observability plane that correlates every error with a trace id. The findings feed back into the SLO, the runbooks and the code.

### The three guards

1. **Burn-rate pause.** The experiment is allowed to spend error budget, because that is what a controlled failure does. The gate fires when the daily burn exceeds 2x the expected rate, and it pauses the experiment on its own.
2. **Suppression windows.** Alerts that the experiment is designed to trigger are silenced for the blast radius and the duration. Nothing outside the radius is silenced.
3. **Trace-id correlation.** Every experiment-induced error carries a tag, so that on-call can separate it from natural failures without a conversation.

The kill switch is a fourth, manual control. It stops the experiment at once and belongs to on-call, not to the scheduler.

### How on-call reads an alert during the window

- A tagged error inside the blast radius is the experiment working. It is logged, not paged.
- An untagged error inside the window is natural. It takes the normal response.
- An error outside the blast radius is natural, because the experiment did not touch it.
- If the burn continues after the pause, the cause is natural, or the experiment broke something that does not recover alone. Run the incident response and roll back the last change.

### What this experiment should teach

The lesson notes that most teams discover their fallback was never fully tested. Record the time from the first rate-limit error to the first successful fallback, and compare it with the SLA. Record whether the gateway's retries amplified the load before the fallback engaged.

### Size the blast radius

Choose a share of the fleet small enough that the fallback capacity on the other providers covers it, and write that share into the experiment definition. A larger share tests more and risks a real outage when the fallback is slower than you believed.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why gate at twice the expected burn and not at any burn? Expected: an experiment is meant to spend some budget. The gate catches the case where it spends far more than planned.
- **Level 4:** The burn keeps rising after the pause. What does that tell you? Expected: the cause is natural, or the experiment broke something that does not recover on its own. Run the incident response and roll back the last change.
- **Level 4:** How do you pick the blast radius for a provider outage experiment? Expected: a share small enough that the fallback capacity covers it, written into the experiment definition and reviewed with on-call.
questions.wrong:
- "Silence all alerts during the experiment." A natural incident in the same window goes unseen. Silence only the blast radius, and keep tagged errors visible.
- "Run it in staging, so no safety plane is needed." Staging cannot show the fallback under real traffic. The safety plane is what makes production acceptable.
- "The burn-rate alert is the kill switch." The alert pauses the experiment. The kill switch stops it at once, and it should be a separate manual control.

questions.title: Set canary gates that do not halt on noise
questions.prompt: You run a canary for a new model. The team wants a rule that stops the rollout when the canary and the baseline differ on any metric. Design the gates so that they catch a real regression and let a healthy rollout through.
questions.short: Write each gate as a multiplier above the baseline, never as equality. Gate on five metrics: latency percentiles, cost per request, error and refusal rate, output length distribution and user feedback rate. Put every threshold above the run-to-run variance, which the lesson measured at up to 15 percent on identical inputs, and hold each step long enough to collect the samples the gate needs.
questions.full:
### Why equality fails

Identical inputs produce different outputs. Floating-point reductions on the GPU run in a different order for each batch shape, the batch size changes between runs, and sampling above temperature zero adds its own randomness. The lesson reports up to 15 percent accuracy variation between runs on the same eval set. "Stable" therefore means inside the expected variance, not identical to the baseline.

### The five gates

| Metric | Breach |
|---|---|
| Latency P50, P95, P99 | canary P99 above 1.5x the baseline |
| Cost per request | more than 20 percent above the baseline |
| Error and refusal rate | 2x the baseline |
| Output length, mean and P99 | a shift in the distribution |
| User feedback, thumbs-down and tickets | 1.5x the baseline |

### Measure the noise floor first

Before the canary, run two arms of the same baseline model and record the spread of each metric between them. That spread is the floor. A gate below it halts every rollout, including a good one. The lesson's exercise asks for the multipliers when the eval noise is plus or minus 7 percent, and the answer is a gate above that band.

### Hold each step long enough

The progression runs 1, 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent. Gates check every 5 to 15 minutes. At 1 percent of a load of 1,000 per minute, the canary sees 10 requests per minute, which is 50 to 150 data points per window. That is enough to read latency and errors, but one or two samples decide the P99, so the P99 gate must hold for more than one window. It is too few for user feedback. Each step must pause until the gate has its samples.

### Keep the exit cheap

A halt is only useful when the rollback is fast. Keep the traffic share in a policy flag and the model in a registry with a pinned digest, so that a breach reverts in seconds.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** How do you learn the size of the noise before the canary starts? Expected: run two canary arms of the same baseline and record the spread of each metric between them.
- **Level 3:** User feedback at the first step is too thin to gate on. What do you do? Expected: gate the early steps on latency, cost, errors and length, and apply the feedback gate from the step that has enough samples.
- **Level 4:** A gate fires at one step, and the metric is normal again on the next check. Continue or halt? Expected: halt and look. A gate that flaps sits inside the noise or sees an intermittent regression, and both need a decision before more users see the model.
questions.wrong:
- "Stop on any difference from the baseline." Two runs of the same model differ, so that rule stops every rollout.
- "Gate on the mean latency." A mean hides the tail. Gate on the percentiles.
- "Allow zero cost increase." A better model can cost more. The lesson sets the breach at 20 percent, and the product decides whether the gain pays for it.

questions.title: How many samples a one percent canary gives a gate
questions.prompt: Your service handles 1,000 requests per minute. The canary opens at one percent, and the gate runs every five minutes. About how many data points does one gate check see, and which gates can you trust at this step?
questions.short: One percent of the 1,000 per minute is 10 requests per minute to the canary, so a five-minute window holds about 50 points and a fifteen-minute window about 150. That is enough to read latency and error rates, and far too few to read user feedback. Gate the first step on latency, cost, errors and output length, and apply the feedback gate at a later step.
questions.full:
### The arithmetic

The lesson's cadence is a gate check every 5 to 15 minutes, depending on volume. At 1 percent of a 1,000 per minute load, the canary receives 10 requests per minute, which gives 50 to 150 data points per window.

### What each gate needs from those points

| Gate | At about 50 points |
|---|---|
| Latency P50 and P95 | readable, with a wide band |
| Latency P99 | one or two samples decide it, so hold more than one window |
| Cost per request | every request reports its tokens, so a large shift shows |
| Error and refusal rate | a baseline of a few percent gives a handful of events, so it is noisy |
| Output length distribution | rough, but a large shift shows |
| User feedback | only some users rate an answer, so a window holds a few ratings at most |

### The next step changes the picture

At 10 percent the canary sees about ten times more points per window. The feedback gate becomes usable there. This is why the progression pauses at each step: the pause is not a formality, it is the time the gate needs to collect its samples.

### Write the dwell rule down

For each step, state the number of windows that must pass with every gate green before the share rises. A gate that needs two windows to confirm a breach doubles the exposure of a real regression, so write that trade-off next to the rule.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** At which step does the user feedback gate become usable? Expected: at 10 percent, where the canary sees about ten times more points per window.
- **Level 2:** Why does a longer window not fix the first step? Expected: a longer window adds points slowly, and a regression runs for the whole window before the gate can fire.
- **Level 3:** Traffic falls to a tenth at night. How does the plan change? Expected: the same share gives about one request per minute, so lengthen the dwell, start at a higher share, or run the ramp during the day.
- **Level 3:** A breach must hold for two windows before the gate fires. What does that cost? Expected: a real regression keeps running through both windows until the halt, so the rule trades fewer false alarms for a longer exposure.
questions.wrong:
- "One percent is safe, so the gates work at one percent." The share is safe for users, and most gates are blind at that sample size.
- "Check every minute for faster detection." A one-minute window at this step holds about ten points, which cannot give a percentile.
- "Start at 25 percent for better statistics." A quarter of the users see the new model before any gate has fired once.

questions.title: What must exist before the first chaos experiment
questions.prompt: A new team wants to run its first chaos experiment against the model service next week. What do you check for before you agree, and what goes wrong when one piece is missing?
questions.short: Five things have to be in place: service level indicators with objectives, observability with traces, metrics and logs, an automated rollback, structured runbooks and an on-call owner. Each one lets you measure the experiment, stop it or repair the damage. When one is missing, the experiment is not a test. It is an incident that you scheduled.
questions.full:
### The five prerequisites

1. **SLI and SLO.** Without a target you cannot say whether the experiment hurt anything.
2. **Observability.** Traces, metrics and logs on a dashboard. You must see the effect while it happens.
3. **Automated rollback.** The policy-flag rollback from the progressive delivery lesson. A rollback that needs a redeploy is too slow for an experiment.
4. **Runbooks.** Structured sections: symptom, hypothesis, verify, act. The on-call reads them under pressure.
5. **On-call.** Someone who responds when the experiment finds something.

### The first experiments

Start with one pod kill of a decode replica under steady traffic, and watch the rerouting and the recovery. If that looks safe, graduate to network chaos. The first model-specific experiment is one provider returning rate-limit errors for a few minutes, to see the fallback engage. Most teams learn here that their fallback was never fully tested.

### The cadence

Weekly small experiments in staging or on a small share of production. Monthly game day on one scenario with a postmortem. Quarterly cross-team audit with a dependency map.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Which experiment goes first, and why? Expected: kill one decode replica under steady traffic, because it tests rerouting and recovery with a small blast radius.
- **Level 2:** Name one failure a generic network chaos tool cannot reproduce for a model service. Expected: a KV cache eviction storm under burst load, or a prompt that stalls the tokenizer.
- **Level 2:** Why does the rollback matter more than the dashboard during an experiment? Expected: the dashboard shows the harm, and the rollback stops it. Without the rollback the harm continues until someone fixes it by hand.
- **Level 3:** The team wants staging only. When is production the right place? Expected: when staging cannot reproduce the traffic shape, the cache state or the provider behavior, and only with the safety guards in place.
questions.wrong:
- "Skip the prerequisites and learn by doing." Without an SLO, a rollback and an on-call owner, the experiment is an outage that you caused on purpose.
- "A dashboard is observability." Chaos needs traces, metrics and logs with trace-id correlation, so that you can tell experiment failures from natural ones.
- "Run the biggest experiment first to find the biggest risk." Start with one replica kill, then grow the blast radius.

questions.title: Order the checks before a paid model call
questions.prompt: You are about to share a public link to a model demo. Every request that reaches the model costs money. Design the sequence of checks a request passes before the model runs, and give the HTTP status for each refusal.
questions.short: Run the cheap checks first and the paid step last. Refuse an oversized body from its `Content-Length` header before you read it, check the access token, take one token from the client's rate bucket, parse and validate the JSON, charge the daily usage cap, and only then call the model. Each refusal returns a JSON error with a stable code, a message and a hint, and the statuses in that order are 413, 401, 429, 422 and 503.
questions.full:
### Why the order matters

A bad request stops at the first check that it fails, and that check should cost the server almost nothing. The model call is the only step that costs money, so it comes last. The browser can repeat some checks with `maxlength` and `required`, but those help honest users only. Any client can send a request without the page, so the server repeats every check.

### The sequence

| Step | Refusal | Status |
|---|---|---|
| route exists | unknown endpoint | 404 |
| `Content-Length` present and numeric | missing, or not a number | 411, 400 |
| body size under the limit | over 4,096 bytes, refused before the read | 413 |
| body arrives in time | client stops sending | 408 |
| access token, when configured | missing or wrong | 401 |
| token bucket per client | bucket empty, with `Retry-After` | 429 |
| content type and JSON object | wrong type, or not an object | 415, 400 |
| fields | missing, empty, too long, control characters | 422 |
| daily usage cap | the day's budget is spent, with `Retry-After` | 503 |
| model call | | 200 |

The cap is charged after validation, so that only valid requests count against the day.

### The error shape

Every refusal has the same JSON body: a `code` that client code and tests compare, a `message` that states the fact with its numbers, a `hint` with one action, and a `request_id` that joins a user report to one log record.

### Two limits, not one

The token bucket bounds each client: a capacity for the burst and a refill rate for the long run. It does not bound the total. A hundred clients that each stay under the limit can still spend the whole budget, so the usage cap counts all model calls in a day and refuses after a fixed number.

### Behind a proxy

The bucket key is the client address. Behind a reverse proxy every request arrives from the proxy, so all clients share one bucket. Read the client address from the header that your own proxy sets, and trust that header from the proxy only.

### Log every request

One record per request, in the `finally` block, including the refused ones: the route, the status, the error code, the latency and the input length. The client address becomes a keyed hash. The text is never stored, and the page says so.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does the usage cap come after the field checks? Expected: so that only valid requests count against the day's total.
- **Level 2:** Why refuse on the header before reading the body? Expected: it stops a large upload before the server spends memory and time on it.
- **Level 3:** Behind a reverse proxy one heavy user gets everyone rate limited. Why? Expected: every request arrives from the proxy address, so all clients share one bucket. Read the client address from the proxy's header, and trust it from the proxy only.
- **Level 3:** What does the server do with a refused body before it answers 413? Expected: it reads and discards up to 64 KiB, because a close with unread data can trigger a TCP reset and the client loses the reply.
questions.wrong:
- "Validate the text first, then check the size." Reading the body before the size check spends the cost that the check exists to avoid.
- "A rate limit is enough, skip the cap." A per-client limit bounds each client. A hundred clients under the limit still spend the whole budget.
- "Return 500 with the stack trace, developers can read it." A stranger cannot act on a stack trace. An error needs a code, a fact and one next action.

questions.title: Pick an observability stack without locking in
questions.prompt: Your team must choose an observability stack for a new model service. Half the team wants an all-in-one platform with evals, prompt versions and session replays. The other half wants a thin gateway that records every call and nothing more. How do you decide, and which pattern lets you avoid the choice?
questions.short: Decide on four axes: the framework you run on, the license you can accept, the budget, and whether you must self-host. A bundled development platform fits a team that iterates on prompts and needs evals tied to traces. A gateway or telemetry tool fits a team that needs portable instrumentation that does not depend on a framework. The pattern that avoids the choice is to emit OpenTelemetry spans with the GenAI conventions from every call and ship them to more than one place: a gateway for day-to-day, an eval platform for regressions, and an archive for long-term analysis.
questions.full:
### Two categories of tool

Development platforms bundle observability with evals, prompt management, dataset versioning and session replay. You run experiments, compare prompts and regression-test a new prompt against old winners. Gateway and telemetry tools record the prompt, the response, the tokens, the latency, the model and the cost, and they stop there.

### The four axes

| Axis | Question |
|---|---|
| stack | one framework, a raw SDK, or several vendors |
| license | open source only, a source-available license, or commercial |
| budget | a free tier, a team plan, or an enterprise contract |
| self-host | required, welcome, or never |

### The trap

Instrumenting inside the agent framework ties the traces to that framework. Instrumenting at the HTTP or SDK layer is portable, so a change of framework or a second framework does not lose the history.

### The glue pattern

1. Emit OpenTelemetry spans with the GenAI conventions from every model call.
2. Route them to a gateway or telemetry tool for the daily view.
3. Ship a copy to an eval platform for regressions.
4. Archive them in a data lake for long-term analysis.

Every tool that reads the conventions can read the same spans, so the stack is a routing decision, not a rewrite.

### What to insist on in either case

- Prompt versions tied to traces. When production regresses, you must be able to bisect to the prompt change that caused it.
- An eval strategy. Tracing without evaluation is expensive logging.
- A sampling policy at scale, because full retention at volume is more expensive than the calls it records.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why instrument at the SDK layer rather than inside the framework? Expected: framework hooks tie you to the framework. The SDK layer keeps working when you change frameworks or add a second one.
- **Level 3:** What breaks when prompt versions are not tied to traces? Expected: when production regresses you cannot bisect to the prompt change that caused it.
- **Level 4:** You ship the same spans to two backends. What do you check so that they agree? Expected: the same conventions version, the same sampling rules on both exporters, and one source of truth for cost attribution, so that two dashboards do not show two bills.
questions.wrong:
- "Pick the tool with the most features." Features you do not use cost money and couple you. Pick on stack, license, budget and hosting.
- "Tracing is enough, evals can come later." Traces without evals are logs with a price. A regression hides in them until a user reports it.
- "The gateway records every call, so skip the platform." A proxy sees calls, not agent steps or sessions. It misses the multi-step traces that an agent regression needs.

questions.title: Detect that the questions changed when the evals did not
questions.prompt: Your eval scores have been flat all year. A product owner tells you that what users ask has changed a lot since spring. How do you detect that change from telemetry, and what do you do with the result?
questions.short: Embed the prompts, pool them per week, and compare the week with a trailing baseline using a population stability index or a KL divergence. A rising score means the input distribution moved, even when the scores on your fixed eval set did not. Alert above a threshold, then sample and label prompts from the new distribution, refresh the eval set, and recheck routing and prompts against it.
questions.full:
### Why the evals cannot see it

An eval runs the model on a fixed, labeled set. It measures the model on last spring's questions. When the questions change, the eval set does not, so the score stays flat while the product quietly serves a different population.

### The detector

The capstone runs a weekly job. It pools the prompt embeddings of the week and computes the PSI against the trailing 4-week baseline. The key terms table gives the usual reading: a PSI above 0.2 signals a meaningful shift. The sample output shows a quiet week at 0.08, below that threshold. The same job can use a KL divergence on the same embeddings. Track the eval score trend next to it, so that both views sit on one page.

### Per application, not only global

A global score averages the drift away. The capstone's exercise computes the PSI per application id, which shows which surface moved. A support bot and a code assistant rarely drift together.

### What to do with a real shift

1. Sample prompts from the new distribution, label them, and refresh the eval set.
2. Rerun the evals on the refreshed set. A flat score on the old set says nothing about the new one.
3. Recheck anything trained or tuned on the old distribution: a routing classifier, the prompt templates, the cache thresholds.

### Where it lives

In the observability plane: spans land in the span store, the weekly job reads them, writes a metric, and the alert chain picks it up.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** What is the difference between a PSI on prompts and a falling eval score? Expected: the PSI measures the inputs, the eval measures the model on fixed inputs, and the first can move while the second stays flat.
- **Level 2:** Why run the detector per application id? Expected: a global score averages the drift away, and the per-application view shows which surface moved.
- **Level 3:** What goes wrong with a one-week baseline? Expected: weekly seasonality looks like drift, and the baseline moves along with the inputs it should measure.
- **Level 3:** The PSI crossed the threshold after a marketing campaign. Is that a problem? Expected: it is a real shift in the inputs. The question is whether quality held on them, so sample, label and evaluate.
questions.wrong:
- "Flat eval scores mean no drift." The eval set is fixed, so it cannot see the inputs change.
- "Compare the raw prompt strings." Wording varies on every request. Embeddings capture the topic distribution.
- "Alert on any score above zero." Small values are noise. The capstone's threshold is 0.2.

questions.title: Why a higher eval score still needs an experiment
questions.prompt: Your new prompt scores higher than the old one on your labeled set. A product manager asks why you still want a randomized online test before the full launch. Give the two-minute version.
questions.short: An eval tells you whether the model can do the task on a fixed, labeled distribution. A randomized test with live users tells you whether users notice and care. A prompt can win on the labeled set and move no product metric, or move it the wrong way. You need both: the eval blocks a regression before any user sees it, and the experiment confirms the product effect after.
questions.full:
### Two different questions

An eval runs offline on a labeled set with a judge, which can be a rubric, a model or a person. It answers: is the output correct, helpful and safe on this distribution?

An A/B test runs online with live users assigned at random. It answers: does the variant move the user-level metric that matters, such as retention or task completion?

### Why one is not enough

Every senior engineer can name a feature that shipped because it felt better, with no experiment. Many of them regressed a product metric that nobody watched for months. The eval cannot see user preference. The experiment cannot catch a regression before exposure. Each one covers the blind spot of the other.

### What to test online

The lesson names three testable axes:

1. Prompt wording and structure. Metrics: task success, retention, cost per request.
2. Model choice. Metrics: task accuracy, cost per request and latency P99 together.
3. Generation parameters such as temperature and top-p. Metric: task-specific.

### The order

Eval first. Then shadow and a canary to prove the variant is stable. Then an A/B test at a 50 percent split when the variant is a distinct alternative. When it is only an improved version of the same behavior, the canary can go to 100 percent without the A/B step. Improved means that the eval showed the gain. The canary gates do not measure task completion, so the skip trusts the eval for it.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Name one metric an experiment produces that an eval cannot. Expected: a user-level metric such as retention, conversion or the thumbs-down rate.
- **Level 2:** The canary passed, and the experiment shows a small drop in conversion. Ship? Expected: not by default. Write the escalation criterion before the test starts, and treat a negative primary metric as a stop.
- **Level 2:** When do you skip the experiment after a canary? Expected: when the new version is an improvement of the same behavior, not an alternative with a different cost curve or tone.
- **Level 3:** Why does model non-determinism change the sample size? Expected: identical inputs give different outputs, so the effective sample is smaller than the nominal one. The lesson multiplies the required sample by about 1.3 to 1.5.
questions.wrong:
- "The eval set is larger, so it is more reliable." The eval set is fixed and labeled, and it measures correctness, not what users prefer.
- "Run the experiment and skip the eval to save a week." Without the eval, a regression reaches users before anyone can see it.
- "If the eval and the experiment disagree, the experiment is wrong." They measure different things. A correct answer that users dislike is a real result.

questions.title: Catch a leaking prompt within five minutes
questions.prompt: A regression ships. One of your prompts starts to leak fake customer identifiers in about one answer in a hundred. Design the observability pipeline so that an alert reaches a person within five minutes of the first bad answer, and say what each stage adds to that clock.
questions.short: Instrument every model call with GenAI-convention spans and ship them over OTLP to a collector. Run a cheap pattern check on every output at the collector, run a judge over the sampled traces on a short schedule, write the scores back as eval spans, export the aggregates as metrics, and alert when the leak score crosses a threshold. The five minutes are the sum of the scrape interval, the judge batch window and the alert routing, so each stage has to be short, and the sampler must keep enough traffic to see a one-in-a-hundred event. The five-minute target covers only the leaks that the pattern flags or the sampler keeps.
questions.full:
### The stages and their share of the clock

| Stage | What it adds | Time it costs |
|---|---|---|
| instrumentation and OTLP export | the span with the output | seconds |
| collector with tail sampling | the decision to keep the trace | seconds, plus the buffer wait |
| pattern check on the output | an instant flag for identifier shapes | none worth counting |
| judge over sampled traces | a score for leaks the pattern misses | the batch window |
| eval spans and metrics export | the aggregate the alert reads | the scrape interval |
| alert rule and routing | the page | the evaluation interval plus routing |

The capstone's eval job reads the last fifteen minutes of sampled traces. For a five-minute target, the judge has to run every minute on the newest traces, or the batch window alone eats the budget.

### Make the rare event visible

At one leak in a hundred, a sampler that keeps a tenth of the successes sees one leak in a thousand answers. At high volume that is fine, and at low volume it is blind. Run a pattern check for identifier shapes on every output at the collector, as the production application capstone does in its output guardrail, and keep every trace that the check flags. The judge then scores the paraphrased leaks on the sampled share only. A paraphrased leak in an unsampled trace gets no score and fires no alert.

### The alert chain

Eval scores land as eval spans linked to the parent trace. A metrics exporter aggregates them, an alert rule fires when the leak score in a window crosses the threshold, and the alert manager routes warnings to chat and critical breaches to the pager.

### Prove it

The capstone's regression probe injects a bug that leaks fake identifiers in one percent of answers and measures the time from deployment to the alert. Detection is the part of the recovery that the dashboard owns. The fix is the rollback, and that belongs to the release path.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Which stage usually dominates the five minutes? Expected: the judge batch window. A job that runs every fifteen minutes cannot meet a five-minute target.
- **Level 3:** The sampler drops nine of every ten successes. What happens to detection when the leak rate is one percent? Expected: it sees one leak in a thousand answers, so at low traffic the detection takes longer. Keep every trace that a cheap pattern check flags.
- **Level 4:** How do you prove the pipeline meets the target? Expected: inject the regression on purpose, as the capstone does, and measure the time from the deployment to the alert.
questions.wrong:
- "Run the judge on every trace." At volume that costs more than the model calls. Sample, and filter with a cheap check first.
- "A daily eval report is enough." A day of leaked identifiers is the incident. The target is minutes.
- "The pattern check catches everything." Patterns miss paraphrases. The judge catches what the pattern misses, and the pattern keeps the judge affordable.

questions.title: Read the prompt router's experiment assignment
questions.short: The code hashes the user id plus the experiment name, takes the result modulo 100, and sends the users whose bucket falls below the traffic percentage to the variant. The hash is deterministic, so one user lands in the same arm on every request for the life of the experiment. The experiment name in the hash keeps the buckets of two experiments independent, so the users who saw the variant in one test are not the same users in the next. With a traffic percentage of 10, about a tenth of the users see the variant on every request all week, and the others never do.
questions.full:
### Line by line

1. The default version is `v1`, so a template with no experiment always resolves.
2. The loop finds the experiment for this template and stops at the first match. One experiment per template at a time.
3. The bucket is a hash of `user_id:exp_name`, read as an integer and reduced modulo 100. That gives a value from 0 to 99.
4. A bucket below `traffic_pct` gets the variant, and every other bucket gets the control.
5. The template renders with the request variables.

### Why the hash is deterministic

The lesson is explicit: hash the user id, do not draw at random. A random draw per request would flip one user between the two prompts, so the user would see two behaviors and the per-user metrics would mix both arms. A stable arm per user also makes the exposure count a count of users, which the experiment analysis needs.

### Why the experiment name is in the key

Without it, the bucket of a user is the same in every experiment, so the same tenth of the users would be the variant group every time. Experiments would be correlated, and the effects of one would carry into the next. The experiment name acts as a salt that gives each experiment its own split.

### What to watch

- The modulo 100 gives steps of one percent. A smaller share needs a larger modulus.
- The demo runs 1000 synthetic user ids through the selector and prints the control and variant shares. That is a cheap sample ratio check, and it belongs in a test.
- The `break` means that a second experiment on the same template never runs. The config shape makes that visible, but nothing warns you.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does a user stay in the same arm across requests? Expected: the hash of the same user id and experiment name gives the same bucket every time.
- **Level 2:** Two experiments are configured for the same template. What happens? Expected: the loop takes the first match and breaks, so the second experiment never assigns anyone.
- **Level 3:** Why not hash the user id alone? Expected: the same users would land in the variant of every experiment, so the experiments would be correlated and carry-over effects would mix the results.
- **Level 3:** How does the demo check the split, and what would you add? Expected: it runs 1000 synthetic ids through the selector and prints both shares. Add the same check on real exposure logs as a sample ratio check.
questions.wrong:
- "A random draw below the percentage would be simpler and the same." It assigns per request, so one user flips between arms and sees both prompts.
- "The hash function is weak, so the assignment is broken." The hash is not a security control here. It only has to be deterministic and well spread.
- "The percentage is the share of requests." It is the share of users, because the bucket is per user and stays fixed.

questions.title: Trace retention when traces cost more than the model
questions.prompt: Your service makes more than a million model calls a day. Keeping every trace now costs more than the model calls themselves. Design a retention policy that keeps the traces you will need during an incident and drops the rest.
questions.short: Sample by rule, not by a flat rate. Keep every errored trace and every high-cost trace, keep a small share of the successes, and keep the aggregates always. Make the decision at the collector with a tail sampler after the trace completes, so that the rule can see the status and the cost. The capstone keeps all errored traces and 10 percent of the successes.
questions.full:
### Why a flat rate fails

A flat 5 percent keeps 5 percent of the errors too. The trace you need in an incident is the one you dropped, and the aggregate error count tells you only that it existed.

### The rules

| Class | Keep |
|---|---|
| errored traces | all of them |
| high-cost traces, long outputs or expensive models | all of them |
| successes | 5 to 10 percent |
| aggregates | always, from every request |

The observability lesson states the rule as 100 percent of errors, 100 percent of high cost and 5 percent of successes. Aggregates do not need traces: counters and histograms count every request even when the trace is dropped.

### Decide at the tail

Head sampling decides when the trace starts, before anything knows whether it will fail. Tail sampling at the collector decides after the trace completes, so it can read the status, the cost and the eval score. The price is buffer memory at the collector, because whole traces wait until the decision.

### Stratify, and know the bias

The capstone's exercise keeps every trace with a toxicity score above 0.5 plus a 10 percent stratified sample of the rest, and asks you to measure the bias that the sampling adds. Any analysis over sampled traces overweights the classes you kept in full. Weight by the inverse of the sampling rate, or run the per-trace evals on the stratified share only.

### Tier the storage

Spans go to a columnar store for queries, and raw events go to object storage for the long tail. The archive is cheap, and long-term analysis runs there.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does head sampling lose the errors? Expected: it decides before the span ends, so it cannot see the status.
- **Level 2:** What survives from a dropped trace? Expected: the metrics. Counters and histograms count every request, whether or not its trace is kept.
- **Level 3:** Your eval jobs run over the sampled traces. What bias do they inherit? Expected: a sample that keeps all errors overweights failures, so weight by the inverse sampling rate or evaluate the stratified share only.
- **Level 3:** The collector runs out of memory during a burst. Why, and what do you change? Expected: tail sampling buffers whole traces until they complete. Cap the buffer, shorten the decision wait, and shed with a head rule under pressure.
questions.wrong:
- "Sample 5 percent of everything." Most of the errors you need in an incident are gone, and the aggregate tells you only that they happened.
- "Keep everything for a week, then delete it." A week of full traces at this volume is the cost you are trying to remove.
- "Traces are enough, drop the metrics." A percentile over an hour needs every request, which only a histogram gives.

questions.title: Which fixes an operations agent may run alone
questions.prompt: A vendor demo shows an operations agent that repairs incidents on its own. Your director asks which actions you would let such an agent take on the model service without a person in the loop. Draw the line and defend it.
questions.short: Allow a narrow set that was approved in advance: restart a pod, revert one named deployment, scale a pool inside approved bounds, and flip an approved feature flag. Keep everything that changes the shape of the system behind a person: topology, resource limits, new code, access rights and databases. The agent proposes, a person approves the judgment calls, and the safe set grows only as the agent builds a record.
questions.full:
### The two sets

| Safe, automated | Not safe, human only |
|---|---|
| restart a pod | change the service topology |
| revert one specific deployment | modify resource limits |
| scale a pool within pre-approved bounds | deploy new code |
| enable a pre-approved feature flag | change access rights |
| | alter a database |

### What makes an action safe

It is reversible, its blast radius is bounded in advance, and it matches a step in a runbook that a person wrote. The lesson's example incident is a KV cache spike that pushed a serving engine out of memory. A pod restart clears it, and a restart is on the safe list. Raising the memory limit might also clear it, and that change alters how every pod runs from then on, so it stays with a person.

### How an action earns automation

1. Write the runbook in structured form: symptom, hypothesis, verify, act.
2. Give the action a success criterion and a verify step that runs after it.
3. Record every proposal and every human decision.
4. Promote the action from proposed to automatic after a run of incidents where the proposal matched what the person chose.

### The approval gate stays

The architecture is a supervisor over log, metric and runbook agents, a hypothesis with evidence, a human approval, and then an action from the narrow set. Even when two independent models agree on the cause, the approval stays for anything outside the safe set. The lesson is direct about vendors who sell a system that needs no supervision: they are overselling.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why is a scale-up inside bounds safe while a resource limit change is not? Expected: the bounds were approved in advance and the action reverses cleanly. A limit change alters how every pod runs and can trigger the next incident.
- **Level 3:** What has to be true before the agent may run an action unsupervised? Expected: a structured runbook, a verify step with a success criterion, an audit record, and a record of proposals that matched the human decision.
- **Level 4:** The agent restarted the busiest pod during a load spike because a probe failed. Was that inside the rules? Expected: the action was allowed and the trigger was wrong. A restart under load drops the running requests, so the rule needs a condition on load and on the probe type, not only on the action.
questions.wrong:
- "If the agent is accurate enough, let it do everything." Accuracy on past incidents does not bound the damage of one wrong broad action.
- "No automation until the agent is perfect." A restart and a revert are safe today, and they remove the first part of most investigations.
- "An approval step makes the agent useless at night." The agent still does the investigation. The person approves one proposed action instead of starting from the dashboards.

questions.title: Stopping an experiment on the first good morning
questions.prompt: A product manager reads the experiment dashboard every morning and wants to end the test on the first day the variant looks significant. Twenty other experiments run this quarter under the same plan. What is wrong with it, and what do you offer instead?
questions.short: A fixed-sample test assumes one look at a sample size chosen in advance. Looking every day and stopping at the first significant result gives noise many chances to cross the line, so the false positive rate climbs. Offer a sequential test, which stays valid under repeated looks and still allows an early stop on a clear winner. Across many experiments, correct for multiple comparisons, and reduce variance with pre-experiment data so each test needs fewer samples.
questions.full:
### The peeking problem

Classical A/B analysis assumes the sample size is fixed before the test. Each extra look is another test, and a stop at the first significant look selects the noise. The manager's plan is not wrong because it looks often. It is wrong because it decides on a procedure that was not built for repeated decisions.

### Sequential testing

Always-valid sequential procedures, such as the mixture sequential probability ratio test and confidence sequences, control the false positive rate under repeated looks. You can check daily and stop early on a clear winner, and the error rate stays what you set. The lesson's simulator shows the fixed and the sequential boundaries side by side.

### Twenty experiments

At 95 percent confidence, 20 experiments produce about one false positive by chance. Two corrections exist. Bonferroni divides the error rate by the number of tests, which is strict. Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate and is less conservative. Choose by the cost of one false launch against the cost of missing a real win.

### Variance reduction

CUPED regresses out the variance that pre-experiment data explains. The lesson gives a typical reduction of 30 to 70 percent, which raises the effective sample size at no cost in traffic. That is the honest way to shorten a test.

### Two more checks

A sample ratio mismatch check catches a broken assignment before you read any result. Non-determinism in model output lowers the effective sample size, so the lesson multiplies the required sample by about 1.3 to 1.5.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg for the quarter? Expected: Bonferroni when any false launch is costly, Benjamini-Hochberg when you accept a controlled share of false discoveries in exchange for power.
- **Level 3:** What does CUPED need, and what does it give? Expected: it needs a pre-period metric for each unit, and it gives a tighter estimate from the same traffic.
- **Level 4:** A new model needs a larger sample than the quarter allows. What do you change? Expected: pick a primary metric with lower variance, apply CUPED, or extend the test. Do not shorten it by stopping early under a fixed-sample procedure.
questions.wrong:
- "Stopping early is fine when the p-value is small." Under a fixed-sample test, a small p-value on the first day is partly selected noise. Only a sequential procedure keeps that stop valid.
- "Run all the tests at 95 percent and ship the winners." About one winner is a false positive by chance. Correct for multiple comparisons.
- "A longer test is always more reliable." Longer helps only if the assignment is sound. Check the sample ratio first.

questions.title: What the system does with a predicted outage
questions.prompt: A model trained on your logs, GPU temperatures and error patterns predicts most outages ten to fifteen minutes before they happen. The team wants to ship it as a dashboard panel. Design what the system does with a prediction, and defend the design.
questions.short: A prediction with no action is a dashboard, and nobody watches a dashboard at three in the morning. Write a policy per prediction class: page the on-call, drain the suspect node or pool before it fails, or scale within approved bounds, and record every prediction with its outcome. Start with the page, measure the precision on live incidents, and promote a class to an automatic drain only when its false alarm rate is acceptable and a person has approved that drain as a pre-approved action in the runbook.
questions.full:
### The result and its limit

The lesson cites a research result: a model trained on past log lines, GPU temperature readings and API error patterns predicted 89 percent of outages 10 to 15 minutes early on its test set. The lesson's reality check follows at once. Predictions without actuation are dashboards. The operational question is what you do when the prediction fires.

### The design

1. **Classify the prediction.** Which failure is coming: a memory exhaustion, a thermal slowdown, a provider error burst. Attach the confidence.
2. **Map each class to an action.** The lesson's safe set is narrow: restart a pod, revert a deploy, scale within pre-approved bounds. A drain is not on that list, so it needs approval before it runs on its own. Drain the pod from the load balancer and restart it before it falls over. Scale the pool within approved bounds. Page a person with the prediction and the evidence.
3. **Fit the action into the lead time.** A drain plus a replacement must complete inside the ten to fifteen minutes, so the replacement has to be warm already. A cold start of a large model takes minutes and can eat the whole window.
4. **Record outcomes.** Every prediction, its class, the action taken and whether the outage happened. Precision and recall per class come from this log, not from the paper.
5. **Guard the blast radius.** Never run two automatic drains in the same pool at once, and never drain under a load spike without a warm spare.

### Why page first

A page costs sleep. A false drain costs capacity for the drain time. A false scale-up costs money. Until the precision per class is measured in production, the cheapest wrong action is the page. Promote a class to automatic action when its record justifies it, the same ladder the lesson uses for remediation.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** What does a false alarm cost under each policy? Expected: a page costs sleep, a drain costs capacity for the drain time, and a scale-up costs money. Pick the policy per class from that cost against the cost of the outage.
- **Level 4:** The lead time is ten minutes and a replacement replica takes longer to warm. What changes? Expected: keep a warm spare or act earlier on a weaker signal. A drain with no warm replacement moves the outage instead of preventing it.
- **Level 4:** How do you know the predictor still works after the service changes? Expected: track precision and recall per class on live incidents, and retrain when the input distribution shifts.
questions.wrong:
- "Ship the panel and let on-call decide." At night nobody watches a panel. The lesson's point is that a prediction without an action is a dashboard.
- "Automate the drain for every prediction from day one." A false alarm then costs capacity, and nothing has measured the false alarm rate on your traffic.
- "The research number means we will prevent most outages." The number was on a test set. Your precision in production is unknown until you measure it.

questions.title: Should the full prompt live on the span
questions.prompt: Your trace backend can store the full prompt and completion on every model span. The support team wants it on, because they debug tickets from traces. The security team wants it off. What do you decide, and how do you still give support what they need?
questions.short: Keep content capture off, which is the default the conventions recommend. Store prompts and completions in your own store, with access control and a retention period, and record a reference id on the span. Support follows the id from the trace to the content, and the trace backend never holds customer data.
questions.full:
### What the default is

By default a span carries timing and metrics, not prompts or completions. Content capture is opt-in through the stability opt-in variable and separate content variables. When it is on, the content lands in `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages` and `gen_ai.system_instructions`, or in the content events on the span.

### What goes wrong when it is on

Prompts carry personal data, secrets and customer documents. Operators read traces, and the trace backend sets its own retention. The conventions lesson lists "capturing full prompts in spans" as the first way the pattern fails. A trace backend is also an attractive target, because it holds everything in one place.

### The pattern that works

Store the content outside the trace: in your log store or object store, under your own access control, audit log and retention. Put a reference id on the span. The lesson calls this the external-reference pattern, and it is also the defense against content poisoning, because the poisoned text never enters the telemetry store.

### What support gets

The same debugging path with one extra step: trace, span, reference id, content store. The store can redact known patterns on write and log every read. Most tickets do not need the content at all, because the span already shows the model, the tokens, the latency, the tool calls and the status.

### What you give up

A one-click view of the prompt inside the trace UI. That is the price, and it is small next to a trace backend full of customer data.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Which spans may carry raw content when capture is on? Expected: none in production. Keep one rule, references only, so nobody has to decide per span.
- **Level 3:** A developer turns capture on in staging for a day. What is the risk? Expected: staging often replays production prompts, and the backend keeps them for its retention period. Use synthetic prompts or scrub before export.
- **Level 3:** How do you keep the content store from becoming the same leak? Expected: access by role, an audit log of reads, a retention period, and redaction of known patterns before the write.
questions.wrong:
- "Turn it on, the trace backend is internal." Internal operators read traces, and the backend's retention is not your policy.
- "Store a hash of the prompt on the span." A hash shows a repeat but gives support nothing to read. A reference id into a controlled store does both.
- "Keep the content on the span and strip personal data with a regex." Patterns miss, and the span is still the wrong store with the wrong retention.

questions.title: Review one span from a new instrumentation branch
questions.prompt:
A colleague opens a review that adds tracing to the agent. The branch emits this span for every model call. List every problem you find before you approve it.

```json
{
  "traceId": "abcdefabcdefabcdefabcdefabcdefab",
  "spanId": "abcdefabcdefabcd",
  "parentSpanId": "",
  "name": "chat",
  "kind": "INTERNAL",
  "attributes": {
    "gen_ai.operation.name": "chat",
    "gen_ai.request.model": "our_smart_model",
    "gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens": 500,
    "gen_ai.content.prompt": "You are a support agent. The customer's card number is ..."
  }
}
```
questions.short: The span marks a model call as INTERNAL, has no parent, and uses an old attribute name for the input tokens. It omits the provider, the output tokens, the response model and the response id, and it writes the prompt text, with a card number in it, into the trace. Fix the kind and the parent link, use the current attribute names, add the missing attributes, and move the content out of the span.
questions.full:
### The problems, in order of damage

| Line | Problem | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `parentSpanId: ""` | an orphan span; no backend can show which agent step made the call | pass the parent context from the `invoke_agent` span |
| `kind: INTERNAL` | a model call crosses a process boundary | `CLIENT` |
| `gen_ai.content.prompt` | prompt text with customer data in a store that operators read | capture off by default; store content outside and put a reference id on the span |
| `gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens` | the attribute was renamed; backends read `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` | use the current name and add `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens` |
| no `gen_ai.provider.name` | cost and error dashboards cannot split by provider | set it on every model span |
| no `gen_ai.response.model` | with routing, the served model can differ from the requested alias | record what the provider returned |
| no `gen_ai.response.id` | no way to match the span to the provider's own log | record the response id |

### Why the content line is the one to fight over

The conventions say instrumentations should not capture inputs and outputs by default. Capture is opt-in through an environment variable, and the production pattern stores content in your own log store and records a pointer on the span. A prompt with a card number in a trace backend is a data leak with a retention policy you did not choose.

### Why the renamed attribute will come back

The GenAI conventions are still marked as in development, and they have renamed attributes before. Pin the conventions version you emit, set the stability opt-in, and test the attribute names of emitted spans, or the next SDK upgrade reopens this review.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does the empty parent matter more than the wrong kind? Expected: with no parent the span is an orphan, the trace is no longer a tree, and you cannot see which step made the call.
- **Level 3:** The team needs the prompt text to debug failures. What do you offer? Expected: store prompts in a separate store with access control and put a reference id on the span, which is the pattern the conventions recommend for production.
- **Level 4:** How do you keep the old attribute name from returning after an upgrade? Expected: pin the conventions version, set the stability opt-in variable, and add a test that asserts the attribute names on emitted spans.
questions.wrong:
- "It has a trace id and a model name, so it is fine." A trace id alone does not link the span to its parent, and a model name without a provider cannot be attributed.
- "Keep the prompt in the span, it is useful." Prompts carry personal data and secrets into a store that operators read. The default is off, and production stores content outside the span.
- "The two token names are synonyms." Backends read the current name. The old one lands in an unknown attribute, and the token dashboard shows nothing.

questions.title: The token dashboard reads zero after an SDK upgrade
questions.prompt: After a routine upgrade of the tracing SDK, the token usage panels show zero for every model, while request counts and latency panels look normal. Nothing else was deployed. Where do you look first?
questions.short: Look at the attribute names on the spans the service emits now. The GenAI conventions are still marked as in development, and they have renamed attributes before: the input token count moved from `gen_ai.usage.prompt_tokens` to `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`. If the SDK emits the new name and the dashboard queries the old one, every token panel reads zero while counts and latency keep working. Pin the conventions version you emit, and set the stability opt-in so that the names do not move under you.
questions.full:
### Why only the token panels broke

Request counts come from the number of spans, and latency comes from span start and end times. Neither depends on an attribute name. A token panel sums one attribute by its key. A renamed key makes the sum zero, and nothing errors.

### Confirm it in one minute

Pull one raw span from after the upgrade and one from before. Compare the attribute keys. The old key is gone, and the new one carries the numbers.

### Two fixes, in order

1. Change the dashboard queries to the new key. During the transition, sum both keys so that old and new spans show.
2. Stop the names from moving: pin the conventions version in the emitter, set `OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN`, and check the names on every SDK upgrade.

### Prevent the repeat

The capstone's tests assert that the canonical attributes are present on emitted spans. Run them on every dependency upgrade. Add an alert for the shape of this incident: token sum at zero while the request count is above zero.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why did the count and latency panels keep working? Expected: they use span counts and span timing, which do not depend on an attribute name.
- **Level 3:** How do you catch the next rename before production? Expected: a test on emitted spans that asserts the canonical attribute names, run on every dependency upgrade.
- **Level 3:** Should the dashboard read both the old and the new name? Expected: yes for a transition window, as a sum of both. Then remove the old one, so that a future regression stays visible.
- **Level 4:** The backend maps the attributes into its own schema. Does that protect you? Expected: only when the mapping follows the same conventions version. A mapping built for the old name shows the same zero, so test the end-to-end path.
questions.wrong:
- "The models stopped reporting usage." The provider responses did not change. The span emitter did.
- "The backend lost data during the upgrade." The latency panels prove the spans arrive. Only one attribute is missing from the query's point of view.
- "Roll the SDK back and stay there." A pinned conventions version and a test let you upgrade on purpose instead of never.

questions.title: The provider slowed down and your service fell over
questions.prompt: During a provider slowdown, the provider began to return rate-limit errors. Within minutes your own service ran out of memory and crashed, although your incoming traffic had not changed. Reconstruct what happened, and fix the retry policy.
questions.short: The gateway retried every rate-limited call, and each waiting retry kept its connection, its buffers and its request state in memory. The retries multiplied the in-flight concurrency several times over the real traffic, and the memory went with it. Fix the policy with exponential backoff and jitter, a small fixed number of attempts, a cap on in-flight requests, and a fallback chain that fails over instead of waiting.
questions.full:
### The chain of events

1. The provider returns 429 for a share of the calls.
2. The gateway retries each one. Each retry holds a connection, a buffer and the request state while it waits.
3. In-flight requests become the traffic multiplied by the attempts. The chaos lesson names this retry-amplified concurrency.
4. Memory follows the in-flight count, and the service that was healthy a minute ago runs out.

### The retry policy in the production application capstone

Exponential backoff with jitter: wait about 1 second, then 2, then 4, with a random spread added to each wait, and give up after 3 retries with a fallback response. The lesson's table separates the cases:

| Failure | Retry | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| 429, rate limit | yes, with backoff | queue the request and tell the user it is in progress |
| 500, server error | yes, 3 attempts | switch to the fallback model |
| timeout over 30 seconds | yes, 1 attempt | a shorter prompt or a smaller model |

The jitter matters as much as the backoff. Without it, every client retries at the same instant and the provider sees a wave on each cycle.

### Bound the concurrency, not only the attempts

Attempts bound the retries of one request. Nothing bounds how many requests wait at once. Add a cap on in-flight requests at the gateway and a retry budget as a share of traffic. When the cap is reached, fail fast into the queue or the fallback instead of holding memory.

### The fallback chain

Primary model, then a secondary model, then a cached response, then a short unavailable message. Each step trades quality for availability, and the user always gets something.

### Test it before the next slowdown

The chaos lesson's first model-specific experiment injects a provider rate-limit for a few minutes and watches the fallback. Most teams learn there that the fallback was never fully exercised.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does backoff alone not stop the memory growth? Expected: backoff spreads the retries in time, and each waiting retry still holds its state. The fix needs a bound on in-flight requests.
- **Level 3:** What does a queue do that a retry does not? Expected: it stores the request without a connection or a worker, and it gives the user a progress message instead of a timeout.
- **Level 4:** The fallback model is cheaper and weaker. Who decides that it is acceptable, and how do you watch it? Expected: the product owner names the paths that may degrade. Log the fallback rate per path, and alert when it stays high.
questions.wrong:
- "Retry faster so the queue drains before memory runs out." Faster retries raise the request rate against a provider that is already limiting you.
- "Raise the maximum retries so users never see an error." Each attempt holds memory. More attempts multiply the in-flight state.
- "The provider caused the outage, there is nothing to fix here." The provider caused the errors. The retry policy turned them into an outage.

questions.title: Make the next rollback take seconds
questions.prompt: Last quarter a bad model launch took three hours to undo, because the only way back was a new deployment. You own the release path now. Design it so that the next time, the way back takes seconds. Name the pieces and say what each one holds.
questions.short: Separate the policy from the model. Keep the traffic split in a feature flag that a configuration change flips, and keep the model in a registry under a pinned digest that never upgrades on its own. A rollback is then two actions: revert the flag, and point the pin at the previous digest, which also restores the prompt and template version pinned with that model. Nothing is rebuilt and nothing is redeployed.
questions.full:
### Two things change in a launch

1. **The policy.** Which share of traffic goes to which model. It lives in a feature-flag system, and a flip takes seconds.
2. **The model.** The artifact itself. It lives in a registry with a content digest. A pinned digest does not move when a new build appears.

A deployment couples the two: to change the policy you ship a new build. The lesson's rule is blunt: if your stack needs a redeploy to roll back, fix that before you roll anything out.

### The rollback

Revert the flag, set the pinned digest to the previous one, and restore the gate thresholds that went with it. The lesson puts the whole sequence at seconds, against hours for a redeploy. In its opening story, the redeploy took three hours and the flag flip would have taken 30 seconds.

### The same flag runs the canary

The canary share lives in the same flag: 1, 10, 25, 50, 75 and then 100 percent. A gate breach sets the share back to zero. That makes the halt and the rollback the same mechanism, so the path you rehearse on every rollout is the path you use in an incident.

### The tooling shape

A progressive delivery controller on the cluster shifts weights at the service mesh or the ingress. A model-serving platform can carry the canary split itself. A feature-flag service holds the policy. Pick one of each, and keep the old model deployed until the new one has held at 100 percent through the gates.

### Rehearse it

The lesson's exercise asks for a rollback under 60 seconds end to end. Time it in staging on every release, and treat a slower result as a release blocker.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why pin the model by digest and not by tag? Expected: a tag can move to a new build. A digest is immutable, so the rollback target is exactly the model that ran before.
- **Level 2:** What else must revert together with the model? Expected: the gate thresholds, and any prompt or template version that shipped with the model.
- **Level 3:** How do you know the path works before you need it? Expected: rehearse it in staging on every release and time it end to end, against a target such as the lesson's 60 seconds.
- **Level 3:** The new model needs a new engine image. Does the flag still work? Expected: yes, when both images run side by side and the flag chooses between them. The old deployment stays alive until the new one has held at 100 percent.
questions.wrong:
- "Roll back by redeploying the previous image." A redeploy takes hours, and the lesson's point is to separate the rollback from the deployment.
- "Delete the old model a day after the launch." The old model must stay available until the canary has held at full traffic through every gate.
- "A fast rollback makes the gates unnecessary." The gates decide when to roll back. The fast path only limits the damage once they fire.

questions.title: Simulate a shadow, canary and rollback plan
questions.prompt: Take-home. You receive a candidate model, a baseline model, and one week of production request logs with the latency, the token counts and the user feedback of each request. Deliver a rollout plan and a simulator that executes it: a shadow phase, a canary ramp with gates, and a rollback. Inject at least two regressions and show where the plan halts for each one. The logs hold user feedback only for the responses that users saw, so state how the simulator produces feedback for the candidate.
questions.short: Build a simulator that replays the logs through both models, computes the five gate metrics per step, and advances the ramp only when every gate holds for the required number of windows. Set each threshold above the baseline's own run-to-run variance, which you measure by replaying the baseline against itself. Inject a cost regression and a quality regression, and show the step at which each one halts and the rollback that follows.
questions.full:
### What a complete submission contains

1. **The noise floor.** Replay the baseline against itself and report the spread of each metric. This is the floor under every gate.
2. **The gates.** Latency percentiles, cost per request, error and refusal rate, output length distribution, and user feedback rate. Write each as a multiplier above the floor. The lesson's defaults are a P99 above 1.5x, a cost more than 20 percent above the baseline, errors at 2x, a shift in the length distribution, and feedback at 1.5x.
3. **The shadow phase.** The candidate sees every request and returns nothing to a user. Report the cost delta, the length distribution, the refusals and the hard errors against the baseline.
4. **The ramp.** Steps at 1, 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent. Compute the dwell at each step from the samples per window, so that a gate never decides on a handful of points.
5. **The rollback.** Model it as the lesson describes: a flag back to zero and a pin on the previous digest. The simulator shows the step and the time it takes.
6. **Two regressions.** The lesson's exercise injects a 25 percent cost regression, and a strong submission shows it halting at the first step. The second regression lives only in the feedback metric, and the submission shows that it stays invisible at the first step and halts only where the sample is large enough.
7. **A written decision.** The lesson's second exercise: a candidate with a 3 percent accuracy gain and a cost 18 percent above the baseline. Write both policy paths, ship and do not ship, and name who decides.

### What the reviewer looks for

- The floor is measured, not assumed.
- The gates are multipliers, and the thresholds sit above the floor.
- The dwell is computed from samples, not from the clock.
- The regression that the first step cannot see is shown, not hidden.
- The rollback is rehearsed inside the simulation.

### What to keep for production

The gate evaluation code and the noise-floor measurement become the checks of the real canary controller. The replay harness becomes the pre-release test for every future candidate.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** The feedback regression was caught late. Is the plan wrong? Expected: no. It shows the limit of the feedback gate, and the fix is a longer dwell at the step where feedback first has samples, or a proxy metric with more volume.
- **Level 4:** The candidate has the same cost and tone as the baseline. What changes in the plan? Expected: skip the A/B step after the canary, which the lesson makes optional for an improved version of the same behavior.
- **Level 4:** What from the simulator survives into production? Expected: the gate evaluation code and the noise-floor measurement, which become the canary controller's checks.
questions.wrong:
- "Use the lesson's thresholds as they are." The lesson's numbers are defaults. The floor comes from your own baseline.
- "Advance the ramp on a fixed schedule." A ramp that moves on the clock ignores whether a gate had enough samples.
- "Model the rollback as a redeploy." The simulator should model the mechanism you will use, and a redeploy is the mechanism the lesson tells you to remove.

questions.title: What a week in shadow mode proves
questions.prompt: A teammate wants to skip the canary. The new model ran in shadow for a week with no errors and a flat bill, so they call it proven. What does that week show, and what does it leave open?
questions.short: Shadow mode copies the production requests to the candidate and logs its outputs, and no user sees them. It shows that the candidate does not crash, does not refuse more often, does not cost more and does not write longer answers. It cannot show that users prefer the answers, because no user read one. Shadow is a smoke test, and the canary is the first quality test.
questions.full:
### What shadow records

For each request, the candidate output is logged next to the production output:

- the output text, as a diff against production;
- the token counts, which give the cost delta;
- the latency;
- refusals and hard errors.

### What it catches

Cost blow-ups, length regressions, a change in the refusal rate and hard errors. These are the failures that make a launch expensive or embarrassing, and shadow finds them with zero user impact.

### What it misses

A quality change that a user would notice. The candidate output never reaches a person, so there is no thumbs-down, no ticket and no retention signal. A model that gives shorter, cheaper and wrong answers passes shadow.

### What comes next

A canary exposes a growing share of users to the candidate, with a gate at each step. The lesson gates on five metrics: latency percentiles, cost per request, error and refusal rate, the output length distribution, and the user feedback rate. The progression runs from 1 percent to 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent. The first user feedback appears here, not in shadow.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Which signal does shadow give that an offline eval does not? Expected: the behavior of the candidate on the real request mix, including cost and output length per request.
- **Level 2:** Shadow shows the cost per request is 40 percent above production. What do you do? Expected: stop before any canary. A cost more than 20 percent above the baseline is a gate breach, and a model that breaks the unit economics is a rollback case.
- **Level 2:** Why can shadow not measure user feedback? Expected: no user sees the candidate output, so there is nothing for a user to rate or report.
- **Level 3:** Shadow doubles the load on your model service. How do you keep it affordable? Expected: send a fixed share of requests to the candidate instead of all of them, and log the same metrics for that share.
questions.wrong:
- "Shadow passed, so the quality is fine." Shadow has no user, so it measures cost, length, errors and refusals only.
- "Shadow is a canary at zero percent." A canary returns the candidate output to real users and gates on their feedback. Shadow never returns an output to a user.
- "A week in shadow replaces the offline eval." The eval judges correctness on a labeled set. Shadow records behavior on live traffic. They answer different questions.

questions.title: Which agent spans are CLIENT and which are INTERNAL
questions.prompt: You add tracing to an agent. In one run it calls a model API twice, runs two tools inside its own process and sends one request to a tool server on another machine. Which of these operations get a CLIENT span, which get an INTERNAL span, and why does anyone care?
questions.short: A call that leaves the process gets a CLIENT span: the two model API calls and the request to the remote tool server. The agent loop step and a tool that runs in your own process get INTERNAL spans. The kind tells a backend the direction of each call, so it can show which operations left the process and which did not.
questions.full:
### The tree for this run

```text
invoke_agent            INTERNAL
 ├── chat               CLIENT
 ├── execute_tool       INTERNAL
 │    └── remote call   CLIENT
 ├── execute_tool       INTERNAL
 └── chat               CLIENT
```

Every span shares one trace id. Each child carries the id of its parent. That is what makes the run one tree instead of six loose records.

### The rule

CLIENT marks a call across a process boundary: a model provider, a tool server, a hosted agent service. INTERNAL marks the agent's own loop steps and any tool that runs in the same process. The conventions apply the same rule to the agent span itself: an agent that runs as a remote service is CLIENT from the caller, and an in-process agent framework is INTERNAL.

### The attributes that go with each kind

| Span | Attributes |
|---|---|
| model call | `gen_ai.operation.name`, `gen_ai.provider.name`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.response.model`, `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens`, `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`, `gen_ai.response.id` |
| tool call | `gen_ai.tool.name`, `gen_ai.tool.call.id` |
| agent run | `gen_ai.agent.name`, `gen_ai.agent.id` |

### Why it matters

Backends draw a waterfall from the kinds and the parent links. A CLIENT span with no response id cannot be matched to the provider log. A tool span with no parent is an orphan, and you can no longer see which agent step caused the call.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** What joins the spans into one tree? Expected: one shared trace id, and a parent span id on every child.
- **Level 2:** The agent calls a hosted agent service instead of a local one. What kind is that span? Expected: CLIENT, because the agent runs in another process.
- **Level 2:** Which attribute lets a dashboard split cost by provider? Expected: `gen_ai.provider.name`, and multi-provider dashboards break when it is missing.
- **Level 3:** A sub-agent runs inside the same process. Does it start a new trace? Expected: no. It is a child span under the parent agent span, so the whole run stays in one trace.
questions.wrong:
- "Every tool call is a CLIENT span." A tool that runs in your process is INTERNAL. Only the call that leaves the process is CLIENT.
- "The kind is decoration." Backends read the kind to show direction, and the conventions set it per span category.
- "Start a new trace for each tool call, for isolation." Separate traces lose the parent link, so you cannot see which step caused the call.

questions.title: An even split that lands at 47 to 53
questions.prompt: An experiment assigns users evenly to control and variant. After a week the dashboard shows 47 percent of users in control and 53 percent in the variant, and the variant is ahead on the primary metric. What do you conclude, and what do you do next?
questions.short: Do not read the result. A configured even split that delivers 47 to 53 over a week of traffic is a sample ratio mismatch, which means the assignment or the logging is broken and the two groups are no longer comparable. Find the cause in the assignment path, fix it, and start the experiment again.
questions.full:
### What the check says

An assignment hash puts each user into an arm. Over a week, the delivered split should sit very close to the configured one. When it does not, the lesson's answer is blunt: something is broken. Both experiment platform types in the lesson run this check for you, and it belongs in front of every readout.

### Why the win is void

Whatever lost users from one arm can be correlated with the outcome. If slow clients fail before they log an exposure in one arm, that arm looks faster and happier. The measured lift is then the dropout, not the variant. No correction after the fact restores the randomization.

### Where to look
